cards.title: Document Model, BSON & WiredTiger Storage Engine
cards.question: Explain Document Model, BSON & WiredTiger Storage Engine
cards.answer_30s: MongoDB stores flexible schema documents as BSON (Binary JSON, supporting types like Date, ObjectId, Decimal128; max 16MB per document). WiredTiger provides document-level concurrency control, Snappy/Zstd compression, and WAL-style journaling + checkpoints.

code.body: # Max document size is 16MB; use GridFS or S3 for large binaries

cards.typical_use: Storing polymorphic catalogs, CMS content, and event logs.
pitfalls: Flexible schema does not mean no schema—enforce JSON Schema `$jsonSchema` validators at the collection level.

cards.title: Schema Design: Embedding vs Referencing
cards.question: Explain Schema Design: Embedding vs Referencing
cards.answer_30s: Embed subdocuments when data is read/written together, has bounded cardinality (1-to-few), and needs single-document atomic updates. Reference by `_id` when arrays grow unboundedly (1-to-millions) or subdocuments are shared across parents.

code.body: // Embed bounded addresses; reference unbounded audit_logs

cards.typical_use: Avoiding the 16MB document limit and array-growth index rewrites.
pitfalls: Rule of thumb: data accessed together should be stored together.

cards.title: Indexing: Compound (ESR Rule), Multikey, TTL & Partial
cards.question: Explain Indexing: Compound (ESR Rule), Multikey, TTL & Partial
cards.answer_30s: Follow the ESR (Equality, Sort, Range) rule when ordering compound index fields. Multikey indexes index array elements; TTL indexes auto-expire documents via a background thread; Partial indexes save RAM by indexing only matching documents.
cards.typical_use: Eliminating COLLSCAN and in-memory blocking sorts.
pitfalls: Use `.explain('executionStats')` and aim for `IXSCAN` where `totalDocsExamined` is close to `nReturned`.

cards.title: Aggregation Pipeline Optimization
cards.question: Explain Aggregation Pipeline Optimization
cards.answer_30s: Aggregations stream documents through stages (`$match`, `$group`, `$lookup`, `$project`). Place `$match` and `$sort` as early as possible so they leverage indexes, and `$project`/`$limit` early to shrink memory passed downstream (100MB stage limit unless `allowDiskUse: true`).
pitfalls: Avoid `$lookup` across massive sharded collections—pre-join or denormalize critical fields.

cards.title: Replica Sets, Oplog & Read/Write Concerns
cards.question: Explain Replica Sets, Oplog & Read/Write Concerns
cards.answer_30s: A Replica Set has 1 Primary and N Secondaries replicating via the capped `oplog.rs`. `w: 'majority'` ensures writes survive primary failover; `readConcern: 'majority'` prevents dirty/rolled-back reads.
cards.typical_use: Guaranteeing durability during automatic Raft-style leader elections.
pitfalls: Wait for `w: 'majority'` on financial/critical writes; `w: 1` risks rollback if the primary crashes before replication.

cards.title: Sharding & Shard Key Selection
cards.question: Explain Sharding & Shard Key Selection
cards.answer_30s: Sharding distributes collections across shards via `mongos` routers and Config Servers using range or hashed shard keys. A good shard key has high cardinality, even write distribution, and aligns with common query filters (targeted vs scatter-gather).
cards.typical_use: Scaling writes and multi-TB datasets horizontally.
pitfalls: Never use a monotonically increasing field (like timestamp or ObjectId) for ranged sharding—it sends 100% of writes to a single hot chunk!

cards.title: Q: What is the ESR rule for MongoDB compound indexes?
cards.question: Q: What is the ESR rule for MongoDB compound indexes?
cards.answer_30s: A: Order compound index keys as Equality fields first, Sort fields second, and Range filter fields last. Putting a Range field before Sort forces MongoDB to perform an expensive in-memory sort (`SORT` stage capped at 100MB).

code.body: // Query: status == 'open' AND amount > 50 ORDER BY createdAt DESC -> { status: 1, createdAt: -1, amount: 1 }

cards.typical_use: Most important MongoDB indexing interview question.
pitfalls: Remember the 3-letter acronym ESR and explain why Range before Sort breaks index ordering.

cards.title: Q: Does MongoDB support ACID multi-document transactions, and when should you use them?
cards.question: Q: Does MongoDB support ACID multi-document transactions, and when should you use them?
cards.answer_30s: A: Yes, since 4.0/4.2 across replica sets and sharded clusters. However, single-document updates are already atomic and much faster—if you constantly need multi-document transactions, reconsider your document embedding or consider PostgreSQL.

code.body: // Model data so 90% of writes mutate a single document atomically

pitfalls: Transactions carry lock/cache overhead in WiredTiger; keep them short.

cards.title: Q: MongoDB vs PostgreSQL — how do you choose?
cards.question: Q: MongoDB vs PostgreSQL — how do you choose?
cards.answer_30s: A: Choose PostgreSQL for complex relational joins, strict referential integrity, financial transactions, and rich SQL analytics (noting PG JSONB also handles semi-structured data well). Choose MongoDB for rapid polymorphic schemas, huge write-sharded document workloads, and hierarchical objects mapped cleanly to documents.

code.body: // PG JSONB covers many simple document cases without a second DB

pitfalls: Avoid saying 'MongoDB is always faster'—benchmarks depend entirely on schema, indexing, and access patterns.

cards.title: Q: What is inside a MongoDB `ObjectId`?
cards.question: Q: What is inside a MongoDB `ObjectId`?
cards.answer_30s: A: A 12-byte identifier: 4-byte Unix timestamp (seconds), 5-byte random value per process, and 3-byte incrementing counter. Because it starts with a timestamp, ObjectIds are roughly time-sortable and embed creation time without an extra field.
pitfalls: Note that because it leads with timestamp, ranged sharding on `_id` creates hot shards—use hashed `_id` or a better shard key.

cards.title: Q: How do you prevent unbounded array growth in MongoDB?
cards.question: Q: How do you prevent unbounded array growth in MongoDB?
cards.answer_30s: A: Unbounded arrays hit the 16MB limit and force WiredTiger to rewrite the entire document and update every multikey index entry on each push. Fix using the Bucket Pattern (group N events per document) or Subset Pattern (embed latest 10 items, store full history in another collection).

code.body: // Subset Pattern: embed recent 5 reviews on Product, full reviews in Reviews collection

pitfalls: Naming the Bucket Pattern and Subset Pattern demonstrates real MongoDB expertise.

cards.title: Q: What is `COLLSCAN` vs `IXSCAN` vs `Covered Query`?
cards.question: Q: What is `COLLSCAN` vs `IXSCAN` vs `Covered Query`?
cards.answer_30s: A: `COLLSCAN` reads every document on disk/RAM (bad). `IXSCAN` traverses a B-Tree index then fetches matching docs (`FETCH`). A Covered Query satisfies both filter and projection solely from index keys (`totalDocsExamined: 0`, zero heap fetch).

code.body: // Covered query: project only indexed fields and exclude _id: { _id: 0, email: 1 }

pitfalls: Remember `_id` is returned by default—you must explicitly pass `_id: 0` if it's not in the index for a covered query.

cards.title: Q: How do you handle Change Streams in MongoDB?
cards.question: Q: How do you handle Change Streams in MongoDB?
cards.answer_30s: A: Change Streams (`collection.watch()`) tail the replica set oplog in real time using resume tokens, enabling reactive cache invalidation, audit logs, and event-driven syncing without polling.
cards.typical_use: Building real-time CDC pipelines with MongoDB.
pitfalls: Persist the `_id` resume token so consumers resume from the exact event after restarts.
